results.content: Evaluating lesion-specific preprocessing pipelines for rs-fMRI in stroke patients: Impact on functional connectivity and behavioral prediction _Open Access_. Alix Lamouroux, Julie Coloigner, Pierre Maurel, Nicolas Farrugia, Giulia Lioi; Evaluating lesion-specific preprocessing pipelines for rs-fMRI in stroke patients: Impact on functional connectivity and behavioral prediction. Using metrics such as connectivity mean strength and functional connectivity contrast, our results indicate that the stroke-specific pipeline significantly reduces spurious connectivity without impacting behavioral predictions. In this study, we address this gap by comparing different preprocessing pipelines for fMRI data in stroke patients, focusing on their effectiveness in minimizing spurious connectivity and improving the prediction of behavioral outcomes. results.title: Analytical Thresholds and Sensitivity: Establishing RFU Thresholds for Forensic DNA Analysis
results.content: Determining appropriate analytical thresholds (ATs) for forensic DNA analysis is critical to maximize allele detection. Hence, the internal validation data supported the use of the optimized 60% reduced PCR amplification reaction volume of the Qiagen Investigator® Argus X-12 QS Kit as well as the CE sample preparation for producing reliable DNA profiles that comply with the quality assurance standards for forensic DNA testing laboratories, while optimizing the analytical cost. In order to make this panel suitable for forensic genetics laboratories, a validation study has been performed in accordance with the Scientific Working Group on DNA Analysis Methods (SWGDAM) guidelines, including species specificity, reproducibility, sensitivity, and stability tests. There are several questions and multiple choices that the analysts have to face when bio-statistical interpretation processes on DNA mixtures take place, such as: (i) the calculation of analytical and stochastic thresholds [9][10][11], (ii) the evaluation of the most probable number of contributors composing the DNA samples [12][13][14][15][16][17], (iii) the establishment of parameters such as it was gradually replaced. Being able to discern artifacts encountered in the baseline from real allelic peaks is of utmost importance in forensic DNA analysis as it can affect sample interpretation. As a result, the analytical threshold was set to 110 RFU, which has high sensitivity to obtain almost full profiles of 0.063 ng DNA, and has high specificity not to detect most of the pull-up and drop-in peaks. The relevant features include: criteria for identification of mixed specimens, establishing detection and interpretation threshold values, defining allele peaks, defining nonallele peaks, identifying artifacts, consideration of tri-allelic patterns, estimating the minimum number of contributors, resolving components of a mixture, determining when a portion of the mixed profile can be treated as a single source profile, consideration of potential additive effects of allele sharing, impact of stutter peaks on interpretation in the presence of a minor contributor, comparison with reference specimens, and some issues related to the application of mixture calculation statistics. Analyses of the electropherogram data associated with the positive, negative, and reagent blank controls included in 50 different capillary electrophoresis runs validate that this approach could be used to determine run-specific thresholds objectively for use in forensic DNA casework.

results.title: How to compare sensitivity and specificity in in vitro diagnostic tests
results.content: # How to compare sensitivity and specificity in In Vitro diagnostic tests. When **comparing the diagnostic sensitivity and specificity** of two commercial tests, it is **essential to go beyond the percentages given in their instructions for use**. ## What do analytical sensitivity and specificity mean in diagnostic tests? **Sensitivity and specificity** are **statistical measures** that **indicate the probability that a test correctly identifies whether or not a person has a disease**. **Sensitivity** indicates the **ability of a test to correctly detect diseased individuals**. **Specificity** measures the **ability of the test to correctly identify healthy people**, avoiding false positives. ## Factors affecting the sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic tests. For example, comparing a rapid test to a molecular test (which is much more sensitive) will show a lower correlation in terms of sensitivity and specificity than if compared to another rapid test. Therefore, the sensitivity and specificity of the same test may vary from one sample type to another. * **Number of samples**: The reliability of sensitivity and specificity data improves significantly as the number of samples in the validation increases. In the case of molecular diagnostic tests, the technique allows the detection of a specific nucleotide sequence. For example, to compare two products that detect the tuberculosis bacterium and its resistance, we must first consider the results of sensitivity and specificity to detect the bacterium and, subsequently, the concordance of the genotyping to find out if the product is capable of correctly detecting the mutations that make it resistant to certain families of antibiotics. On the other hand, **if the test works with direct sample**, it is **necessary to validate its specific detection capacity in that type of sample**. The **most reliable option** is always to **compare two tests with the same samples and under the same conditions**, or at least to **verify that they have been validated against the same reference technique**. Understanding **how sensitivity and specificity are measured** and **what factors affect these parameters** **allows purchasing decisions to be made based on robust and comparable data.** This is especially **relevant for both healthcare professionals and distributors** who want to offer **reliable products with high clinical value.**.
